title: Constitutional Distillation Protocol
abstract: The Constitutional Distillation Protocol CDP is proposed as a CHOIR primitive for converting explicit institutional governance into implicit specialist behavior, so that specialist kernels behave as though constitutional rules are permanently present rather than receiving those rules as a prompt on every inference § Abstract . The proposal extends prompt distillation from task-specific rule compression into what the source calls institutional reasoning preservation, with the stated result that "governance becomes part of model behavior rather than runtime prompt overhead" § Abstract . It is a research proposal: it defines a five-stage protocol, a two-layer architecture, three hypotheses, four CHOIR-specific evaluation metrics, and three limitations, and it reports no results against any of them.

sections.heading: Abstract
sections.html: The Constitutional Distillation Protocol (CDP) is proposed as a CHOIR primitive for converting explicit institutional governance into implicit specialist behavior, so that specialist kernels behave as though constitutional rules are permanently present rather than receiving those rules as a prompt on every inference (§ Abstract). The proposal extends prompt distillation from task-specific rule compression into what the source calls institutional reasoning preservation, with the stated result that "governance becomes part of model behavior rather than runtime prompt overhead" (§ Abstract). It is a research proposal: it defines a five-stage protocol, a two-layer architecture, three hypotheses, four CHOIR-specific evaluation metrics, and three limitations, and it reports no results against any of them.

sections.heading: Research Question
sections.html:
The source states its problem directly. Modern AI systems repeatedly consume large system prompts containing review policies, safety constraints, reasoning guidelines, formatting requirements, escalation rules, and organizational standards; these "are expensive to transmit, difficult to maintain, and easy to diverge across agents" (§ Problem Statement). The framing claim is set out as a block quotation in the source:

Organizations lose reasoning consistency when governance exists only as text instead of learned behavior.

The question the document sets out to answer follows from this: CHOIR "requires a mechanism that preserves institutional reasoning across every cognitive kernel without duplicating constitutional instructions every inference" (§ Problem Statement). The governing principle proposed as the answer is stated as: "Governance should be internalized, not repeatedly instructed" (§ Core Principle).

The source draws the contrast against a narrow task example rather than against prompt distillation as a field. Under the heading "Instead of distilling:" it quotes "Classify language."; under "We distill:" it quotes "Reason like this institution." (§ Core Principle).

sections.heading: Finding
sections.html:
The document's conclusion is a proposed protocol, not an empirical result. What it establishes is a specification of that protocol together with an explicit account of what would have to be true for it to work and what remains untested.

The five-stage protocol

CDP is defined in five stages (§ Constitutional Distillation Protocol).

StageNameWhat the source specifies
1Constitution DefinitionThe institution defines its constitutional rules — evidence standards, acceptable uncertainty, escalation policies, precedent handling, disagreement protocols, formatting conventions. These become the constitutional prompt.
2Teacher DeliberationA teacher model operates under the full constitution over real organizational decisions and produces constitutionally compliant reasoning.
3Distillation DatasetRuntime prompts are stripped away; the student receives an institutional case as input and teacher-produced reasoning as target.
4Specialist Kernel FormationRole-specific kernels are created rather than a single distilled model.
5Runtime ExecutionNo constitutional prompt is injected; the scheduler decides only role, effort, and rounds.

Stage 1 carries an explicit constraint on the constitutional prompt: it "is not intended for long-term runtime use. Its purpose is to teach" (§ Stage 1 — Constitution Definition).

Stage 2 names the inputs as real organizational decisions — investment memos, QA incidents, architecture reviews, customer escalations, committee discussions — and the teacher's output as conclusions, structured reasoning, citations, uncertainty, objections, and resolutions. The teacher "becomes the institutional exemplar" (§ Stage 2 — Teacher Deliberation).

Stage 3 states that "The student never receives the constitutional prompt directly. Instead, it learns behaviors demonstrated by the teacher." The source states this "mirrors the prompt distillation workflow demonstrated in Tinker" (§ Stage 3 — Distillation Dataset). The source presents the five stages as a flat sequence and does not rank any one of them above the others.

Stage 4 gives a role table, presented in the source as an example rather than a fixed roster (§ Stage 4 — Specialist Kernel Formation):

KernelDistilled behavior
Historianprecedent-first
Librarianevidence discipline
Contrarianassumption challenge
First Principlesdecomposition
Expansionistalternative generation

The stated invariant is that "Every kernel shares the same constitutional foundation while expressing different reasoning roles" (§ Stage 4 — Specialist Kernel Formation).

Stage 5 states the runtime consequence: the constitutional behavior "already exists inside the kernel", so the scheduler's remaining decisions are role, effort, and rounds only (§ Stage 5 — Runtime Execution).

Two-layer architecture

The source separates a Constitutional Layer from a Runtime Layer (§ Architectural Model — Two-Layer System). Layer 1 holds governance, precedent, institutional philosophy, reasoning standards, and escalation policies; the source's characterisation is one sentence: "This layer teaches." Layer 2 contains the Historian, Contrarian, First Principles, Expansionist, and Librarian kernels, which "execute decisions without repeatedly loading constitutional instructions."

Claimed benefits, as stated

The source gives three (§ Why This Matters).

  1. Reduced Prompt Overhead. Long constitutional prompts disappear from runtime; inference becomes cheaper, latency decreases, context remains cleaner. The source ties this to "the efficiency motivation behind prompt distillation" rather than to any measurement of its own.
  2. Consistent Institutional Behavior. Every kernel inherits the same governance, so that CHOIR is composed of "Five constitutionally aligned specialists" rather than "Five differently prompted agents."
  3. Organizational DNA. The source introduces this as a new concept: "The constitutional behavior of an institution becomes a trainable artifact", with investment philosophy, engineering culture, QA methodology, and legal reasoning style given as examples. The distinction drawn is that "Rather than preserving documents— CHOIR preserves demonstrated reasoning."

These are asserted, not demonstrated. No cost, latency, or consistency figure appears anywhere in the source document.

Relationship to the Deliberation Cohort

The source is explicit that CDP "complements—not replaces—the Deliberation Cohort" (§ Relationship to Deliberation Cohorts), and tabulates the division:

Cohort ComponentCDP Contribution
Rolepreserved
Effortpreserved
Roundspreserved
Governanceinternalized

The stated effect is that "Every cohort member begins with constitutional alignment before deliberation starts."

Hypotheses, not results

The three claims are recorded as hypotheses (§ Research Hypotheses), verbatim:

  • H1 — Distilled constitutional behavior reduces prompt tokens while preserving institutional consistency.
  • H2 — Role-specific constitutional distillation produces stronger specialization than a single universal distilled model.
  • H3 — Institutions transfer culture more effectively through demonstrated decisions than through static policy documents.

None of H1, H2, or H3 is tested in the source document. No training run, baseline, or comparison is reported.

Evaluation metrics — named, not operationalized

Alongside accuracy, latency, and token cost, the source names four CHOIR-specific metrics (§ Evaluation Metrics): Constitutional Fidelity (how closely runtime behavior matches teacher behavior), Precedent Compliance (whether reasoning correctly applies historical decisions), Dissent Quality (whether objections improve institutional decisions), and Governance Consistency (whether different kernels apply the same constitutional principles). Each is given a one-line definition. The source supplies no measurement procedure, scoring scale, threshold, or baseline for any of them.

Limitations recorded by the source

The source states that "Prompt distillation inherits important constraints" and records three (§ Limitations):

  • Demonstration Dependence. "A student can only learn behaviors the teacher actually demonstrates." The implication the source itself draws: "Organizations cannot preserve reasoning they have never exhibited."
  • Coverage Risk. "Rare constitutional edge cases require representative examples."
  • Constitutional Drift. "Institutions evolve. Distilled kernels require periodic constitutional refresh cycles."

Citation status

The source's appeals to prior work on prompt distillation are carried by unresolved citation placeholders — <Cite refs={["turn0search0","turn0search1"]}/> and <Cite ref=turn0search0/> — appearing in § Core Principle, § Stage 3 — Distillation Dataset, § Why This Matters (1. Reduced Prompt Overhead), and § Limitations (Demonstration Dependence). The only named prior system is "Tinker" (§ Stage 3 — Distillation Dataset). The document contains no bibliography or reference list, so these citations cannot be resolved from the document as it stands.

Canonical axiom

The document closes with a stated axiom (§ Canonical Axiom):

Governance should not live in prompts.

Governance should live in behavior.

and with the summary claim that "institutional reasoning becomes durable only when governance is transformed from explicit instructions into internalized cognitive behavior shared across every specialist kernel within CHOIR" (§ Canonical Axiom). Note the modality: the source frames this as what the protocol proposes, not as an established result.

sections.heading: Architectural Implications
sections.html:
Only implications the source itself draws are listed here.

  • CHOIR gains a two-layer split. Governance moves out of the runtime path into a separate Constitutional Layer whose function is to teach; the Runtime Layer holds the five named kernels and executes without loading constitutional instructions (§ Architectural Model — Two-Layer System).
  • The runtime scheduler's responsibility narrows. Under CDP the scheduler decides only role, effort, and rounds, because constitutional behavior is already resident in the kernel (§ Stage 5 — Runtime Execution).
  • The Deliberation Cohort's interface is unchanged. Role, effort, and rounds are all preserved; only governance changes status, from injected to internalized (§ Relationship to Deliberation Cohorts).
  • Kernels multiply rather than consolidate. CHOIR creates role-specific kernels — Historian, Librarian, Contrarian, First Principles, Expansionist — instead of one distilled model (§ Stage 4 — Specialist Kernel Formation).
  • Distilled kernels require periodic constitutional refresh. Because institutions evolve, distilled kernels "require periodic constitutional refresh cycles" (§ Limitations — Constitutional Drift), and constitutional versioning is listed as future work (§ Future Research). CHOIR would therefore have to carry a refresh mechanism, which the source does not specify.
  • The institution's decision history becomes a training input. Real organizational decisions — investment memos, QA incidents, architecture reviews, customer escalations, committee discussions — are the corpus the teacher operates over (§ Stage 2 — Teacher Deliberation), which means CHOIR's behavior is bounded by what the institution has actually exhibited (§ Limitations — Demonstration Dependence).

The source names DAALE (Data Algorithmically Analytical Logical Engine) as the engine in its header block, but draws no implication for DAALE anywhere in the body. Any consequence for DAALE is not stated in the source document.

sections.heading: Open Questions
sections.html:
Recorded by the source as future work (§ Future Research):

  • constitutional versioning
  • automatic constitution extraction from decision history
  • on-policy constitutional reinforcement
  • disagreement-aware constitutional updates
  • cross-organization constitutional transfer

Further gaps and untested items the source records or leaves open:

  • H1, H2, and H3 are untested. The source states them as hypotheses and reports no experiment, dataset, model, or measurement against any of them (§ Research Hypotheses).
  • The four CHOIR-specific metrics are undefined operationally. Constitutional Fidelity, Precedent Compliance, Dissent Quality, and Governance Consistency each have a one-line description and no measurement procedure or threshold (§ Evaluation Metrics).
  • Coverage of rare constitutional edge cases is unresolved. The source states such cases "require representative examples" but does not say how such examples are to be identified or produced (§ Limitations — Coverage Risk).
  • The refresh cadence for constitutional drift is unspecified. "Periodic" is the only qualification given (§ Limitations — Constitutional Drift).
  • The prior work is uncited in resolvable form. The claims about prompt distillation rest on placeholder citation tokens and a single product name, "Tinker", with no reference list in the document (§ Core Principle, § Stage 3 — Distillation Dataset, § Why This Matters, § Limitations).
  • The efficiency claims are unquantified. "Inference becomes cheaper. Latency decreases." carry no figures, baselines, or conditions (§ Why This Matters — 1. Reduced Prompt Overhead).
